section_summary: This section traces the tightening and politicization of Japanese press controls from late 1930 through July 1936. It covers the press protest arising from the detention of a Jiji Shimpo reporter, extensive bans concealing military operations and developments in Manchuria, attempts to suppress inflammatory writing, and growing government control of newspapers, correspondents, translators, and news agencies. The closing documents concern the consolidation of Domei Tsushinsha, restrictions on foreign information gathering, and Japan's suppression of the May 1936 issue of Current History.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 96: Press protest against police interference
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the political controversy caused by the detention and interrogation of Jiji Shimpo reporter Hosokoshi.
subfiles.summary: Tokyo newspapers jointly protested after police used Hosokoshi's detention to seek information about General Ugaki's political ambitions and relations with Baron Tanaka. The press resolution denounced censorship, political spying, and intimidation, while Ugaki and the Privy Council also criticized the police. Home Minister Adachi apologized and promised respect for press freedom, but the affair damaged his political position and may have influenced Shidehara's decision to continue as acting prime minister.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to telegram on strict press censorship
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to a telegram concerning strict censorship of the press and correspondents.
subfiles.summary: The sheet refers to telegram No. 77, filed elsewhere under 793.94/4380. Its stated subject is strict censorship over the press and press correspondents in Japan.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 76: Government crisis, Shanghai deployments, and censorship
subfiles.about: Reports rumors of a Japanese government change, additional troop deployments to Shanghai, and strict news censorship.
subfiles.summary: Forbes reports that financial difficulties and military influence were producing rumors of a coalition cabinet despite the government party's electoral victory. Two more divisions were to go to Shanghai, while the movements of Major Bratton and Lieutenant Dusenbury reflected military planning. Strict censorship made reliable news from Japan difficult to obtain.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to telegram on Manchurian troop-movement bans
subfiles.about: Refers to a telegram concerning press bans on Japanese troop movements to Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to telegram No. 164, filed under 893.01-Manchuria/280. Its subject is the suppression of information about Japanese troops moving to Manchuria.

subfiles.title: Department memorandum on Tokyo despatch No. 48
subfiles.about: Recommends reading Tokyo's despatch and its classified list of press bans.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum notes that despatch No. 48 encloses bans imposed on Japanese and foreign newspapers in Tokyo since September 18, 1931. It highlights the covering analysis of restrictions concerning troop and naval movements, Manchuria, and social problems.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 48: Analysis of Japanese press bans
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits and analyzes confidential lists of press bans imposed in Tokyo since the Manchurian Incident.
subfiles.summary: Grew divides the bans into troop movements, naval movements, Manchurian affairs, and social or civil disturbances. He concludes that they concealed frontier defenses, reinforcements, Japan's role in creating and controlling Manchukuo, and plans for communications, finance, and a permanent Japanese garrison. Although domestic publication was tightly controlled, some foreign correspondents could still send banned information abroad.

subfiles.title: Enclosure: Chronological lists of press bans
subfiles.about: Lists individual Japanese press bans issued from September 1931 through June 1932.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure records restrictions on troop and naval movements, including operations toward Shanghai, Manchuria, Sakhalin, and Korea. Other bans concealed Japanese involvement in Manchukuo, communications and financial policy, political violence, the May 15 Incident, leftist activity, agricultural distress, and banking conditions. Several entries also record when particular bans were partly or wholly lifted.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 219: Press bans involving Jehol, Sakhalin, and Manchukuo
subfiles.about: Reports three current press bans and the expected timing of Japanese recognition of Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: The bans prohibited reporting on Jehol and related troop movements, destroyers sent to Sakhalin, and treaty negotiations with Manchukuo. Grew expected the treaty to pass the Privy Council around September 20 and recognition to follow shortly afterward.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to letter on the anti-American press campaign
subfiles.about: Refers to a letter describing an organized Japanese press campaign against the United States.
subfiles.summary: The sheet states that the campaign appeared to be stimulated from a central source. It also records that almost nothing favorable to the United States was being permitted to appear.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 39: Ban on military and naval deployment information
subfiles.about: Reports new censorship orders covering forces destined for China and Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: The principal ban covered the identity, strength, and movement of warships, aircraft, and military units expected to be sent from Japan. Further restrictions concerned experimental aircraft, operational plans in Manchuria and Jehol, and the arrest of General Li's emissaries at Benxi. Only information officially released by the Navy could be published.

subfiles.title: Department analysis of telegram No. 39
subfiles.about: Assesses the legal and military significance of the reported censorship order.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum explains that Article 27 of the Press Law already authorized the War and Navy Ministers to restrict military reporting. It judges that the new orders perfected comprehensive control and placed the press on a wartime basis. Because similar bans had preceded operations, the writer inferred that unusually large military and naval movements might be imminent.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to telegram No. 61
subfiles.about: Refers to a telegram about the March 9 ban on reporting forces destined for China or Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: The sheet repeats the central language of the military and naval press ban. It links the document to file 793.94/6037.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 61: Press ban preceding possible operations
subfiles.about: Connects a March 9 military press ban with the prospect of renewed operations.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports that publication was prohibited concerning warships, aircraft, or unit strength expected to be dispatched from Japan to China or Manchukuo. He notes that similar restrictions had preceded active military operations in the past.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to telegram on Manchukuo–North China negotiations
subfiles.about: Refers to a telegram reporting a ban on comment about negotiations between Manchukuo and North China.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to telegram No. 168 in the Manchuria file. Its subject is the prohibition of commentary on current political negotiations.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 168: Ban on comment about North China negotiations
subfiles.about: Reports a press ban concerning negotiations between Manchukuo and the North China administration.
subfiles.summary: The ban forbade comment on the negotiations. The Embassy had no additional information and repeated the message to Peiping.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to telegram on inflammatory publications
subfiles.about: Summarizes a Foreign Office initiative to prevent provocative books and articles.
subfiles.summary: The sheet records a January 23 interministerial meeting on publications that predicted war or endangered foreign relations. It notes that the Foreign Office intended to stop a particular book then in production.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 18: Plans to prohibit inflammatory books and articles
subfiles.about: Reports an interministerial effort to restrict writings that presaged war or harmed international relations.
subfiles.summary: Representatives of the Foreign, War, Navy, and Home Ministries met on January 23 to consider means of stopping provocative publications by retired officers and others. The Foreign Office told Grew that a book already on the press would be prevented from appearing.

subfiles.title: Japanese Embassy letter transmitting Hirota's policy message
subfiles.about: Transmits an English translation of a telegram from Foreign Minister Hirota on suppressing harmful publications.
subfiles.summary: Saitō states that he had discussed the issue with the President at luncheon and believed the President was strongly interested. The enclosed translation conveyed the Japanese Government's decision to suppress writings considered harmful to foreign relations.

subfiles.title: Translation of Japanese decision on harmful publications
subfiles.from: Kōki Hirota, Minister for Foreign Affairs
subfiles.to: Hiroshi Saitō, Japanese Ambassador in Washington
subfiles.about: Sets out two categories of publications the Japanese Government intended to suppress.
subfiles.summary: The decision covered works revealing or imagining Japanese tactics and strategy in a possible foreign war. It also covered writings asserting the necessity or inevitability of war with a particular country or otherwise exciting foreign opinion.

subfiles.title: Department reading memorandum on inflammatory publications
subfiles.about: Recommends Grew's despatch on Japan's growing concern over inflammatory writing.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum mentions the recent travels of Counts Futara and Soejima and suggests Futara acquired useful ideas abroad. It particularly directs attention to the Foreign Office statement on regulating publications affecting international relations.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 684: Inflammatory publications
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Describes Diet criticism of warlike publications and the government's promise of stricter control.
subfiles.summary: Count Futara, War Minister Hayashi, Jinjirō Mizuno, and former Foreign Minister Yoshizawa warned that imaginary-war stories and provocative books damaged diplomacy and made Japan appear belligerent. Grew observed that such works sold widely and were often inspired by the military, although the military now appeared to think the propaganda had gone too far. The Foreign Office promised stricter censorship of works revealing war techniques, provoking foreign nations, or instigating war.

subfiles.title: Department memorandum on the Japan Advertiser
subfiles.about: Provides background on the finances and independence of the Japan Advertiser before presenting reports on news control.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum recounts financial aid supplied after the 1923 earthquake by Lamont, Rockefeller, and Crane so that B. W. Fleisher could rebuild an independent American-oriented newspaper. After another fire in 1930, Fleisher rejected Japanese financing offered through figures including Takuma Dan and Finance Minister Inoue because he feared political obligations. The writer believed Fleisher would close the paper rather than accept a government subsidy.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 955: Control of news by the Japanese Government
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits differing foreign-correspondent assessments of increasing Japanese control over news.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports complaints from Wilfred Fleisher and James R. Young while noting that Associated Press representative Glenn Babb considered Japanese censorship comparatively reasonable. All agreed that the planned consolidation of the major news agencies suggested preparation for tighter control during the anticipated crisis of 1935–36. Grew also wondered whether his own efforts against anti-American inflammatory writing had encouraged broader government intervention.

subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 1: Statement by Wilfred Fleisher
subfiles.from: William T. Turner, recording Wilfred Fleisher's statement
subfiles.about: Records pressure on the foreign-owned Japan Advertiser to adopt a more cooperative position toward Japan.
subfiles.summary: Fleisher described a merger suggestion from Shigeru Yoshida, criticism from Foreign Office spokesman Eiji Amau, and threatened reductions in advertising by the South Manchuria Railway and Mitsui. He believed official tolerance of foreign reporting was gradually narrowing. The newspaper had rejected a tentative government subsidy and preferred closure to loss of independence.

subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 2: Statement by James R. Young
subfiles.from: William T. Turner, recording James R. Young's statement
subfiles.about: Records Young's view that restrictions and official pressure on foreign reporting had recently increased.
subfiles.summary: Young said Japanese sources had become reticent after official reprimands and that the Foreign Office had rebuked him over several stories. He asserted that much Japanese press material, including claims about American activity in China, originated in the War Office, which he called Japan's most active propaganda factory.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to telegram on the Manchurian oil monopoly
subfiles.about: Refers to a telegram reporting suppression of news about the proposed Manchurian oil monopoly.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies telegram No. 236 and the associated Manchuria file. Its stated subject is a Japanese ban on publication of oil-monopoly news.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 236: Manchurian oil monopoly and the open door
subfiles.about: Reports Eiji Amau's statements on Manchukuo and a press ban covering the proposed oil monopoly.
subfiles.summary: Amau reportedly argued that protests should be addressed either to Manchukuo or China, that the Nine-Power Treaty did not apply, and that open-door declarations could be withdrawn. A press ban prevented direct Japanese reporting on the Manchurian oil monopoly, apparently to counter foreign publicity. Newspapers nevertheless mentioned diplomatic representations from Washington and London without directly naming the monopoly.

subfiles.title: Report No. 292: Censorship of newspapers
subfiles.about: Assesses the severity and uneven operation of Japanese newspaper censorship, especially over naval information.
subfiles.summary: The report states that the Foreign, War, Navy, and Home Ministries could impose one of the world's strictest censorship systems. Naval reporting had become so vague that newspapers sometimes fabricated policy news, while bans were enforced more strictly against major Tokyo and Osaka dailies than provincial papers. The writer concludes that almost no useful military information would appear during wartime.

subfiles.title: Department reading note on cartoons of chiefs of state
subfiles.about: Recommends Grew's short despatch on caricatures of foreign leaders in Japanese newspapers.
subfiles.summary: The note calls attention to despatch No. 1626. It identifies cartoons of chiefs of state in the Japanese press as the document's principal subject.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1626: Cartoons of chiefs of state
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits Japanese newspaper cartoons after protests over a Vanity Fair depiction of the Japanese emperor.
subfiles.summary: Grew invokes the warning that people in glass houses should not throw stones and sends examples of Japanese treatment of foreign leaders. The Interior Ministry reportedly ordered newspapers not to caricature foreign sovereigns or chiefs of state after a German protest over depictions of Hitler. Grew notes that the order was widely disregarded.

subfiles.title: Kokumin clipping on Roosevelt's congressional message
subfiles.about: Reports President Roosevelt's warning that worsening international affairs could produce a great war.
subfiles.summary: The translated headline emphasizes Roosevelt's fear that unfavorable international trends might lead to general war. A note explains that the article itself summarizes the President's message to Congress.

subfiles.title: Yomiuri clipping on Hitler and an aerial Locarno pact
subfiles.about: Uses a hostile headline to describe Hitler's reported conditions for joining an aerial Locarno agreement.
subfiles.summary: The headline calls Hitler overbearing and attributes to him demands for Europe's strongest air force and the restoration of former German possessions. It illustrates the kind of caricaturing or provocative treatment discussed in Grew's covering despatch.

subfiles.title: Jiji Shimpo clipping on Hitler's reported demands
subfiles.about: Reports that Hitler's firm position had obstructed negotiations over an aerial Locarno agreement.
subfiles.summary: The translated headlines characterize Hitler's terms as brazen demands and say the agreement had struck a snag. The clipping also includes a British government denial that Hitler made new demands.

subfiles.title: Department summary of increased control of news
subfiles.about: Summarizes Embassy despatch No. 1775 on new Japanese controls over news collection and distribution.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum highlights the government-sponsored merger of Nippon Dempo into Domei Tsushinsha and interprets the resulting agency as a vehicle for the approved Japanese version of events. It also notes police suppression of the Okayama translation service, arrests of Soviet and Chinese Embassy translators, pressure on foreign correspondents, and possible restrictions on trade information. The writer expected diplomatic and consular information gathering to become substantially harder.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1775: Increased control of news in Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Provides a comprehensive report on government efforts to control news agencies, translators, correspondents, and foreign information gathering.
subfiles.summary: Grew describes the forced amalgamation of Nippon Dempo with the partly official Domei Tsushinsha, predicting that it would distribute approved domestic and international propaganda and restrict incoming foreign news. Police closed the Okayama translation service and arrested translators employed by the Soviet and Chinese Embassies, apparently to obstruct the flow of information. The despatch also covers censorship of foreign correspondents, Gerald Sampson's arrest and deportation, proposed controls on commercial information, and expanded surveillance of foreigners. Grew concludes that measures directed mainly against Soviet organizations would also impede other diplomatic missions and news agencies.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to despatch No. 1876 on press restriction bills
subfiles.about: Refers to a report on restrictions created by the Seditious Literature and Mobilization Secrets bills.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies despatch No. 1876 and points to file 894.20/166. It characterizes the legislation as a further restriction of the Japanese press.

subfiles.title: Current History inquiry about suppression of its May issue
subfiles.about: Requests information about Japan's suppression of the May 1936 issue of Current History.
subfiles.summary: Casman reports that the New York post office had informed the magazine that its May issue was suppressed in Japan. He encloses mention of a communication to the Japanese Ambassador and asks the Department for any available explanation.

subfiles.title: Department acknowledgment of Current History inquiry
subfiles.from: Wilbur J. Carr for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the magazine's inquiry and promises an Embassy investigation.
subfiles.summary: Carr states that the Department possessed only newspaper reports about the suppression. He says the American Embassy in Tokyo had been asked to determine and report the facts.

subfiles.title: Instruction to investigate the Current History ban
subfiles.about: Orders the Embassy to investigate suppression of the May issue of Current History.
subfiles.summary: The Department asks the Embassy to ascertain the relevant facts. It directs that the report be returned through naval radio at Shanghai.

subfiles.title: Washington Times clipping: Japan seizes magazines
subfiles.about: Reports the confiscation at Kobe of copies of Current History's May issue.
subfiles.summary: The clipping says Kobe postal authorities apparently seized the magazine because it contained articles about Japanese affairs. Publisher M. E. Tracy sought explanations from the Department of State and the Japanese Embassy after receiving notice through New York and Seattle.

subfiles.title: Department memorandum on the Current History inquiry
subfiles.about: Clarifies the relationship between Current History's letter and the Washington Times report.
subfiles.summary: Michael J. McDermott states that the Department received no inquiry beyond the magazine's July 14 letter. He believes the July 20 Washington Times item referred to that same communication.

subfiles.title: Relayed Tokyo telegram on the Current History ban
subfiles.from: Clarence E. Gauss, Shanghai, relaying Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the Embassy's findings on why Current History's May issue was denied distribution.
subfiles.summary: The local distributor was officially told that the issue could not circulate, although no specific offending article was named. The agent said foreign publications were routinely banned in this manner. Embassy inquiries suggested that references to the February 26 Incident triggered the ban, but this explanation could not be verified.

subfiles.title: Department's final reply to Current History
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Provides the magazine with the Embassy's explanation for suppression of its May issue.
subfiles.summary: Welles reports that the Japanese agent was ordered not to distribute the issue and was not told which article was objectionable. He explains that the magazine apparently discussed the February 26 Incident, during which several Japanese statesmen were assassinated. Because police had prohibited mention of that incident, the Department believed the suppression was lawful under Japanese law.
